subject: Career
title: Receiving Feedback Without Defensiveness
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Receiving Feedback Without Defensiveness.

hook.text: Your body tenses. Your mind races for counterarguments. Feedback triggers a threat response — literally.

buildup.text: The amygdala treats criticism like a physical threat. Fight-or-flight activates before reason can engage.

discovery.text: Sheila Heen's research: separate the 'what' (content of feedback) from the 'who' (your feelings about the giver).

twist.text: Even poorly delivered feedback often contains a kernel of truth. Mining for that kernel is the skill.

climax.text: Pause. Say 'Thank you. Let me think about that.' Process later when your threat response has calmed.

punchline.text: The best feedback is the hardest to hear. Listen anyway.

quiz.question: Why is receiving feedback difficult according to neuroscience?
options: The amygdala treats criticism as a physical threat

details.summary: Receiving feedback without becoming defensive is a skill that requires separating your identity from your work output. Defensiveness shuts down learning and signals to others that giving you honest input is not safe, reducing the quality of feedback you receive over time.
details.whyItMatters: People who receive feedback well get promoted faster because colleagues and managers invest more in their development. Openness to feedback creates a virtuous growth cycle.
takeaways: Separate your identity from your work when hearing feedback
Thank the giver before responding to create a positive loop
Ask clarifying questions instead of defending your perspective

faq.question: Why do I become defensive even when I know the feedback is valid?
faq.answer: Defensiveness is an automatic identity-protection response. Your brain interprets criticism of your work as criticism of you. Recognizing this mechanism in the moment allows you to pause, breathe, and shift into a learning stance before responding.

faq.question: What should I say when I receive feedback I disagree with?
faq.answer: Start by thanking the person and paraphrasing what you heard. Then ask for a specific example. Even if you ultimately disagree, the act of exploring their perspective often reveals a kernel of useful truth you would have missed through immediate rebuttal.
